facts.quote: subdivision: *A. siemensiiDames, 1897 A. albersdoerferiKundrat et al., 2018

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 150 million years ago.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx lived in the Late Jurassic around 150 million years ago

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx was first named based on a single feather discovered in 1861.
facts.quote: It was named from a single feather in 1861

facts.statement: Twelve additional fossils of Archaeopteryx have been discovered since the initial announcement.
facts.quote: Over the years, twelve more fossils of Archaeopteryx have surfaced

facts.statement: It is debated whether all discovered remains of Archaeopteryx belong to a single species or at least a single genus.
facts.quote: most experts regard all the remains that have been discovered as belonging to a single species or at least genus, although this is still debated

facts.statement: Despite having broad wings and an inferred ability to fly or glide, Archaeopteryx shared more features with small Mesozoic dinosaurs than with modern birds.
facts.quote: Despite their small size, broad wings, and inferred ability to fly or glide, Archaeopteryx had more in common with other small Mesozoic dinosaurs than with modern birds

facts.statement: The presence of feathers in Archaeopteryx suggests it may have been warm-blooded.
facts.quote: feathers (which also suggest warm-bloodedness)

facts.statement: All known Archaeopteryx fossils originate from limestone deposits near Solnhofen, Germany.
facts.quote: All of the fossils come from the limestone deposits, quarried for centuries, near Solnhofen, Germany.

facts.statement: The initial Archaeopteryx specimen was the first dinosaur found to possess feathers.
facts.quote: The initial specimen was the first dinosaur to be discovered with feathers.

facts.statement: A single Archaeopteryx feather was found in 1860 or 1861 and described by Hermann von Meyer in 1861.
facts.quote: The initial discovery, a single feather, was unearthed in 1860 or 1861 and described in 1861 by Hermann von Meyer.

facts.statement: In 2019, laser imaging suggested the initial feather specimen came from a different dinosaur than the body fossils because its morphology was inconsistent with other known Archaeopteryx feathers.
facts.quote: In 2019 it was reported that laser imaging had revealed the structure of the quill (which had not been visible since some time after the feather was described), and that the feather was inconsistent with the morphology of all other Archaeopteryx feathers known, leading to the conclusion that it originated from another dinosaur.

facts.statement: The first Archaeopteryx skeleton, known as the London Specimen, was unearthed in 1861 near Langenaltheim, Germany.
facts.quote: The first skeleton, known as the London Specimen (BMNH 37001), was unearthed in 1861 near Langenaltheim, Germany

facts.statement: The London Specimen, missing most of its head and neck, was described by Richard Owen in 1863 as Archaeopteryx macrura.
facts.quote: Missing most of its head and neck, it was described in 1863 by Richard Owen as Archaeopteryx macrura

facts.statement: The Berlin Specimen was discovered in 1874 or 1875 by farmer Jakob Niemeyer near Eichstätt, Germany.
facts.quote: The Berlin Specimen (HMN 1880/81) was discovered in 1874 or 1875 on the Blumenberg near Eichstätt, Germany, by farmer Jakob Niemeyer.

facts.statement: In 1897, Wilhelm Dames named the Berlin Specimen as the new species A. siemensii.
facts.quote: In 1897 it was named by Dames as a new species, A. siemensii

facts.statement: The Maxberg Specimen was discovered in 1956 near Langenaltheim.
facts.quote: The Maxberg Specimen (S5) was discovered in 1956 near Langenaltheim

facts.statement: Florian Heller brought the Maxberg Specimen to attention in 1958 and described it in 1959.
facts.quote: it was brought to the attention of the German paleontologist Florian Heller in 1958 and described by him in 1959.

facts.statement: The Haarlem Specimen was discovered in 1855 near Riedenburg, Germany.
facts.quote: The "Haarlem Specimen" (TM 6428/29, also known as the Teylers Specimen) was discovered in 1855 near Riedenburg, Germany

facts.statement: John Ostrom reclassified the Haarlem Specimen in 1970, and it is now located at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem, the Netherlands.
facts.quote: It was reclassified in 1970 by John Ostrom and is currently located at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem, the Netherlands.

facts.statement: In 2017, the Haarlem Specimen was named the separate genus Ostromia, considered closely related to Anchiornis from China.
facts.quote: In 2017 it was named as a separate genus Ostromia, considered more closely related to Anchiornis from China

facts.statement: Further analyses suggest the Haarlem Specimen differs little from certified Archaeopteryx except for a markedly larger size.
facts.quote: More in-depth analyses and consultation of the original depictions of the fossil in a more intact state confirmed that what remains of the animal differs little from certified Archaeopteryx except by a markedly larger size

facts.statement: The Eichstätt Specimen was discovered in 1951 near Workerszell, Germany, and described by Peter Wellnhofer in 1974.
facts.quote: The Eichstätt Specimen (JM 2257) was discovered in 1951 near Workerszell, Germany, and described by Peter Wellnhofer in 1974.

facts.statement: In 2007, Phil Senter classified Jurapteryx, A. siemensii, and A. bavarica as junior synonyms of A. lithographica.
facts.quote: In 2007, Phil Senter classified Jurapteryx, A. siemensii and A. bavarica as junior synonyms of A. lithographica

facts.statement: The Unnumbered Specimen was discovered in the 1970s near Eichstätt, Germany, and described in 1988 by Wellnhofer.
facts.quote: The ('Unnumbered Specimen') was discovered in the 1970s near Eichstätt, Germany, and described in 1988 by Wellnhofer.

facts.statement: The Munich Specimen was discovered on August 3, 1992, near Langenaltheim and described in 1993 by Wellnhofer.
facts.quote: The Munich Specimen (BSP 1999 I 50, formerly known as the Solenhofer-Aktien-Verein Specimen) was discovered on 3 August 1992 near Langenaltheim and described in 1993 by Wellnhofer.

facts.statement: The Daiting Specimen was discovered in 1990 in the younger Mörnsheim Formation at Daiting, Suevia.
facts.quote: An eighth, fragmentary specimen was discovered in 1990 in the younger Mörnsheim Formation at Daiting, Suevia.

facts.statement: A fragmentary fossil known as the Bürgermeister-Müller Specimen was found in 2000.
facts.quote: Another fragmentary fossil was found in 2000.

facts.statement: The Thermopolis Specimen was discovered in Bavaria and described in 2005 by Mayr, Pohl, and Peters.
facts.quote: The Thermopolis Specimen (WDC CSG 100) was discovered in Bavaria and described in 2005 by Mayr, Pohl, and Peters.

facts.statement: The eleventh specimen, known as the Altmühl Specimen, was announced in 2011 and described in 2014.
facts.quote: The discovery of an eleventh specimen was announced in 2011; it was described in 2014.

facts.statement: The Schamhaupten Specimen was discovered in 2010 at the Schamhaupten quarry and announced in February 2014.
facts.quote: The Schamhaupten Specimen had been discovered by an amateur collector in 2010 at the Schamhaupten quarry, but the finding was only announced in February 2014.

facts.statement: A fossil previously considered the Mühlheim Specimen was described in 2019 and reassigned to the genus Alcmonavis.
facts.quote: When the specimen was scientifically described in 2019, it was thus reassigned to a distinct genus Alcmonavis.

facts.statement: The Karlsruhe Specimen was published in January 2025 and originates from the Mörnsheim Formation.
facts.quote: A thirteenth specimen, SMNK-PAL 10,000 or Karlsruhe Specimen, was published in January 2025, this one from the Mörnsheim Formation.

facts.statement: The Chicago Specimen was first informally announced in 2024 by the Field Museum in Chicago.
facts.quote: The existence of a fourteenth specimen (the Chicago Specimen) was first informally announced in 2024 by the Field Museum in Chicago, US.

facts.statement: In 2025, Jingmai O'Connor and colleagues published a study describing the Chicago Specimen, reporting the first known tertials in Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: In 2025, the paleornithologist Jingmai O'Connor and colleagues officially published a study describing this fourteenth specimen, reporting the first known tertials (specialized inner secondary flight feathers) and other novel features in Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: The Munich Specimen is missing only the front of its face.
facts.quote: Only the front of its face is missing.

facts.statement: The Thermopolis Specimen has the best-preserved head and feet, but most of the neck and lower jaw are not preserved.
facts.quote: It has the best-preserved head and feet; most of the neck and the lower jaw have not been preserved.

facts.statement: The Schamhaupten Specimen is the only known specimen lacking preserved feathers.
facts.quote: It is the only specimen lacking preserved feathers.

facts.statement: The Thermopolis Specimen shows that Archaeopteryx lacked a reversed toe, implying a terrestrial or trunk-climbing lifestyle rather than the ability to perch on branches.
facts.quote: It shows that Archaeopteryx lacked a reversed toe—a universal feature of birds—limiting its ability to perch on branches and implying a terrestrial or trunk-climbing lifestyle.

facts.statement: Studies of the eleventh specimen revealed previously unknown plumage features, including feathers on the upper and lower legs and metatarsus, as well as the only preserved tail tip.
facts.quote: Palaeontologists of LMU Munich studied the specimen, which revealed previously unknown features of the plumage, such as feathers on both the upper and lower legs and metatarsus, and the only preserved tail tip.

facts.statement: Analyses suggested the Mühlheim Specimen belongs to a more advanced avialan lineage close to Jeholornis and the ancestors of Sapeornis.
facts.quote: However, subsequent analyses strongly suggested it belongs to a markedly more advanced avialan lineage and may even be quite close to Jeholornis and the ancestors of short-tailed birds such as Sapeornis.

facts.statement: The Unnumbered Specimen was originally classified as Compsognathus by the amateur collector Friedrich Müller.
facts.quote: It originally was classified as Compsognathus by an amateur collector, the same mayor Friedrich Müller after which the museum is named.

facts.statement: The Schamhaupten Specimen is from the Painten Formation and is somewhat older than other specimens.
facts.quote: It is from the Painten Formation and somewhat older than the other specimens.

facts.statement: In 1985, a group led by Fred Hoyle and Lee Spetner claimed that the feathers on the Berlin and London Archaeopteryx specimens were forged.
facts.quote: Beginning in 1985, an amateur group including astronomer Fred Hoyle and physicist Lee Spetner, published a series of papers claiming that the feathers on the Berlin and London specimens of Archaeopteryx were forged.

facts.statement: Alan J. Charig and colleagues at the Natural History Museum in London rejected the claims that the Archaeopteryx specimens were forged.
facts.quote: Their claims were repudiated by Alan J. Charig and others at the Natural History Museum in London.

facts.statement: Alan J. Charig and others cited hairline cracks running through both rock and fossils, plus pre-discovery mineral growth, as proof that the feathers were original.
facts.quote: Charig et al. pointed to the presence of hairline cracks in the slabs running through both rock and fossil impressions, and mineral growth over the slabs that had occurred before discovery and preparation, as evidence that the feathers were original.

facts.statement: Spetner et al. failed to account for the fact that cracks found in the slabs were old and filled with calcite, preventing natural propagation through any alleged cement layer.
facts.quote: Spetner et al. then attempted to show that the cracks would have propagated naturally through their postulated cement layer, but neglected to account for the fact that the cracks were old and had been filled with calcite, and thus were not able to propagate.

facts.statement: Analysis of the London specimen revealed a non-rock substance identified as likely silicone rubber residue from mould-making, rather than cement.
facts.quote: They also attempted to show the presence of cement on the London specimen through X-ray spectroscopy, and did find something that was not rock; it was not cement either, and is most probably a fragment of silicone rubber left behind when moulds were made of the specimen.

facts.statement: Palaeontologists generally dismiss the forgery claims because they were based on geological misunderstandings and ignored other feather-bearing specimens.
facts.quote: Their suggestions have not been taken seriously by palaeontologists, as their evidence was largely based on misunderstandings of geology, and they never discussed the other feather-bearing specimens, which have increased in number since then.

facts.statement: Most Archaeopteryx specimens were found in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany, dating to the early Tithonian stage of the Jurassic period (150.8–148.5 million years ago).
facts.quote: Most of the specimens of Archaeopteryx that have been discovered come from the Solnhofen limestone in Bavaria, southern Germany, which is a Lagerstätte, a rare geological formation known for its highly detailed fossils laid down during the early Tithonian stage of the Jurassic period, approximately 150.8–148.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx was roughly the size of a raven, featuring broad, rounded wings and a long tail relative to its body.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx was roughly the size of a raven, with broad wings that were rounded at the ends and a long tail compared to its body length.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx feathers were structurally very similar to those of modern birds.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx feathers, although less documented than its other features, were very similar in structure to modern-day bird feathers.

facts.statement: Unlike modern birds, Archaeopteryx possessed small teeth and a long bony tail, traits shared with contemporary dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Unlike modern birds, Archaeopteryx had small teeth, as well as a long bony tail, features which Archaeopteryx shared with other dinosaurs of the time.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx had three separate digits on each forelimb, each ending in a claw.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx had three separate digits on each fore-leg each ending with a "claw".

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx specimens featured well-developed, markedly asymmetrical flight feathers with a barb-barbule-barbicel arrangement similar to modern birds.
facts.quote: Specimens of Archaeopteryx were most notable for their well-developed flight feathers. They were markedly asymmetrical and showed the structure of flight feathers in modern birds, with vanes given stability by a barb-barbule-barbicel arrangement.

facts.statement: Body plumage in Archaeopteryx is poorly documented and has only been properly studied in the Berlin specimen.
facts.quote: The body plumage of Archaeopteryx is less well-documented and has only been properly researched in the well-preserved Berlin specimen.

facts.statement: The Berlin specimen shows well-developed leg feathers resembling contour feathers, though some are decomposed and lack barbicels.
facts.quote: In the Berlin specimen, there are "trousers" of well-developed feathers on the legs; some of these feathers seem to have a basic contour feather structure, but are somewhat decomposed (they lack barbicels as in ratites).

facts.statement: A patch of symmetrical, firm pennaceous feathers ran along the back of the Berlin specimen, similar to modern bird contour feathers but less stiff than flight feathers.
facts.quote: A patch of pennaceous feathers is found running along its back, which was quite similar to the contour feathers of the body plumage of modern birds in being symmetrical and firm, although not as stiff as the flight-related feathers.

facts.statement: Feather traces on the Berlin specimen included a fluffy, decomposed "proto-down" that may have appeared fur-like in life, similar to that found in Sinosauropteryx.
facts.quote: Apart from that, the feather traces in the Berlin specimen are limited to a sort of "proto-down" not dissimilar to that found in the dinosaur Sinosauropteryx: decomposed and fluffy, and possibly even appearing more like fur than feathers in life (although not in their microscopic structure).

facts.statement: No feathers were found on the upper neck and head of the Berlin specimen, though this may be due to preservation artifacts rather than nudity.
facts.quote: There is no indication of feathering on the upper neck and head. While these conceivably may have been nude, this may still be an artefact of preservation.

facts.statement: Most Archaeopteryx specimens likely drifted on their backs in shallow sea water before burial, leading to a characteristic 'death pose' with the head, neck, and tail bent downward.
facts.quote: It appears that most Archaeopteryx specimens became embedded in anoxic sediment after drifting some time on their backs in the sea—the head, neck and the tail are generally bent downward, which suggests that the specimens had just started to rot when they were embedded, with tendons and muscle relaxing so that the characteristic shape (death pose) of the fossil specimens was achieved.

facts.statement: In 2011, researchers conducted the first color study on an Archaeopteryx specimen.
facts.quote: In 2011, graduate student Ryan Carney and colleagues performed the first colour study on an Archaeopteryx specimen.

facts.statement: A 2013 study suggested that Archaeopteryx may have had complex light- and dark-colored plumage based on sulphate distribution.
facts.quote: In a 2013 study published in the Journal of Analytical Atomic Spectrometry, new analyses of Archaeopteryxs feathers revealed that the animal may have had complex light- and dark-coloured plumage

facts.statement: An author from a previous color study argued against using biomarkers to indicate eumelanin in the full Archaeopteryx specimen.
facts.quote: An author on the previous Archaeopteryx colour study argued against the interpretation of such biomarkers as an indicator of eumelanin in the full Archaeopteryx specimen.

facts.statement: In a 2020 study, Carney and colleagues argued against a 2013 interpretation and demonstrated that an isolated covert feather was entirely matte black.
facts.quote: Carney and other colleagues also argued against the 2013 study's interpretation of the sulphate and trace metals, and in a 2020 study published in Scientific Reports demonstrated that the isolated covert feather was entirely matte black

facts.statement: In 1954, Gavin de Beer concluded that the London specimen was the holotype of Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: In 1954 Gavin de Beer concluded that the London specimen was the holotype.

facts.statement: In 2007, scientists petitioned the ICZN to designate the London specimen as the neotype of Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: In 2007, two sets of scientists therefore petitioned the ICZN requesting that the London specimen explicitly be made the type by designating it as the new holotype specimen, or neotype.

facts.statement: The ICZN upheld the suggestion to designate the London specimen as the neotype on October 3, 2011, after four years of debate.
facts.quote: This suggestion was upheld by the ICZN after four years of debate, and the London specimen was designated the neotype on 3 October 2011.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx fossils date to the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Jurásico Superior

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx is classified in the Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Sauropsida, Superorder Dinosauria, Order Saurischia, Suborder Theropoda, Family Archaeopterygidae, and Genus Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Sauropsida superordo: Dinosauria ordo: Saurischia subordo: Theropoda unranked_familia: Paraves familia: Archaeopterygidae genus: Archaeopteryx

facts.statement: The recognized species of Archaeopteryx include A. albersdoerferi (Kundrat et al. 2018), A. lithographica (Meyer, 1861), and A. siemensii (Dames, 1897).

facts.statement: The name Archaeopteryx derives from the Ancient Greek words for 'ancient' and 'wing' or 'feather'.
facts.quote: El nombre deriva del griego antiguo ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos), que significa «antiguo», y πτέρυξ (ptéryx), que significa «pluma» o «ala».

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx has generally been accepted by paleontologists as the oldest known bird and a member of the group Avialae.
facts.quote: Desde el ha sido generalmente aceptado por los paleontólogos, y señalado en las obras de consulta como el ave más antigua conocida (miembro del grupo Avialae).

facts.statement: Researchers have identified potentially older avialans, including Anchiornis, Xiaotingia, and Aurornis.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, se han identificado aviales potencialmente más antiguos, incluyendo a Anchiornis, Xiaotingia y Aurornis.

facts.statement: At the time Archaeopteryx lived, Europe was an archipelago of islands in a warm, shallow tropical sea much closer to the equator than it is today.
facts.quote: durante un momento en que Europa era un archipiélago de islas en un mar tropical cálido poco profundo, mucho más cerca del ecuador de lo que está ahora.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx was similar in shape to a European magpie, with larger individuals possibly reaching the size of a crow.
facts.quote: Similar en forma a una urraca europea, con individuos más grandes, posiblemente, alcanzasen el tamaño de un cuervo.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx could grow to about 0.5 meters (1 foot 8 inches) in length.
facts.quote: Archaeopteryx podría crecer a alrededor de 0,5 m (1 pie con 8 pulgadas) de longitud.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx had feathers, which also suggest endothermy, along with various skeletal characteristics.
facts.quote: plumas (que también sugieren homeotermia) y diversas características del esqueleto.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx was named based on a single feather in 1861.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado a partir de solo una pluma en 1861.

facts.statement: Over the years, fossils of ten other Archaeopteryx specimens have been discovered.
facts.quote: A lo largo de los años se han descubierto fósiles de otros diez ejemplares de Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: While most experts consider all discovered remains to belong to a single species despite variations, this is still a subject of debate.
facts.quote: a pesar de la variación entre estos ejemplares, la mayoría de los expertos consideran que todos los restos que se han descubierto son pertenecientes a una única especie, aunque esto todavía es objeto de debate.

facts.statement: Most of the eleven fossils include impressions of feathers.
facts.quote: La mayoría de los once fósiles incluyen impresiones de plumas.

facts.statement: Because these feathers are of an advanced form (remiges), these fossils are evidence that feather evolution began before the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: Debido a que estas plumas son de una forma avanzada (remeras), estos fósiles son evidencia de que la evolución de las plumas se inició antes del Jurásico Superior.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Archaeopteryx was discovered just two years after Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo de Archaeopteryx fue descubierto tan solo dos años después de que Charles Darwin publicara El origen de las especies.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx lived during the Early Tithonian age of the Jurassic period, approximately 150.8 to 148.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx was about the size of a crow, with broad wings rounded at the tips and a long tail relative to body length.

facts.statement: It could reach a maximum length of fifty centimeters, with an estimated weight of 0.8 to 1 kilogram.
facts.quote: Podía llegar a un máximo de cincuenta centímetros de longitud, con un peso estimado de 0,8 a 1 kilogramo.

facts.statement: The feathers of Archaeopteryx, though less documented than its other features, are very similar in structure and design to the feathers of modern birds.
facts.quote: Las plumas del Archaeopteryx, aunque menos documentadas que sus otras características, son muy similares en su estructura y diseño a las plumas de aves de hoy en día.

facts.statement: Despite having numerous avian traits, Archaeopteryx also possessed many characteristics of theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Pese a la presencia de numerosos rasgos aviares, no obstante, el Archaeopteryx tenía muchas características de los dinosaurios terópodos.

facts.statement: Unlike modern birds, Archaeopteryx had small teeth and a long bony tail, characteristics it shared with other dinosaurs of the time.
facts.quote: A diferencia de las aves modernas, Archaeopteryx tenía pequeños dientes, así como una larga cola ósea, características que compartía con otros dinosaurios de la época.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx had certain avian traits, such as a keel, flight feathers, wings, and a partially reversed first toe, alongside typical theropod characteristics.
facts.quote: tenía ciertos rasgos avianos, como la espoleta, plumas de vuelo, alas y un primer dedo del pie parcialmente puesto al revés, junto a características típicas de los terópodos.

facts.statement: For example, it has a long ascending process in the heel, interdental plates, an obturator process of the ischium, and long chevrons in the tail.
facts.quote: Por ejemplo, tiene un largo proceso ascendente en el talón, placas interdentales, un proceso obturador del isquion y largos cheurones en la cola.

facts.statement: In particular, Ostrom considered Archaeopteryx to be notably similar to the theropod family Dromaeosauridae.
facts.quote: En particular, Ostrom consideró que Archaeopteryx era notablemente similar a la familia de terópodos Dromaeosauridae.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx specimens are notable for their well-developed flight feathers.
facts.quote: Los especímenes de Archaeopteryx son notables por sus bien desarrolladas plumas de vuelo.

facts.statement: The body plumage of Archaeopteryx is less documented and has only been properly investigated in the well-preserved Berlin specimen.
facts.quote: El plumaje corporal de Archaeopteryx está menos documentado y solo ha sido investigado con propiedad en el bien preservado espécimen de Berlín.

facts.statement: There is no indication that Archaeopteryx had feathers on the top of the neck and head.
facts.quote: no hay indicación de que hubiera plumas en la parte superior del cuello y la cabeza.

facts.statement: The feathers of Archaeopteryx are completely modern in structure.

facts.statement: Archaeopteryx belongs to the parent group Avialae.
